title: OOM Mitigation & Circuit Breaker Playbook (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a pragmatic playbook for detecting, mitigating, and recovering from runtime memory-related failures (GPU/host OOM, kernel aborts) and cascading error patterns. It couples low-level kernel/kv-cache tactics with higher-level controls (retries, circuit breakers, admission) so the serving runtime can keep serving useful responses with predictable SLAs under memory pressure.

Scope:
- Applies to model-serving workers (GPU and CPU), model variants (fp16, int8), and the routing layer that decides fallbacks.
- Focused on transient and sustained memory pressure events: per-request OOMs, cumulative KV cache growth, and kernel-level aborts.
- Not an infra-scaling document (e.g., autoscaling policies are referenced but not replaced).

Goals:
1) Detect memory-pressure early and classify it (transient vs sustained).
2) Prefer graceful degradation (smaller model, lower max-tokens, reduced batch-size) over hard failures.
3) Avoid noisy retries that exacerbate pressure.
4) Provide clear SRE runbook steps and automated mitigations with observable state.

Assumptions and constraints:
- Workers expose memory telemetry (GPU free, host RSS, per-kernel allocation traces).
- Models are registered with memory profiles (peak working set for typical seq lengths, kernel memory factors).
- Kernel library supports at least two memory/compute tiers for most ops (stable low-memory kernels and fast high-memory kernels).
- Some fallback actions (e.g., CPU fallback) have significant latency cost and are last-resort.

Failure modes we care about:
- Immediate per-request OOM: single request triggers allocation > available → kernel abort or process OOM.
- Accumulating pressure: many requests gradually fill KV cache or native pinned buffers → eventual OOM for new requests.
- Kernel crash/segfault from unsupported kernel variant or driver bug.
- GC-like thrashing: frequent allocation/deallocation cycles causing fragmentation and slowdowns.
- Backpressure cascade: retries from clients or the router push more load into a stressed pool.

Detection signals (sources):
- Kernel return codes / driver OOM errors (NV_PROF / CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY).
- Worker-level OOM exit / cgroup OOMKill events.
- Sudden drop in successful token throughput + spike in per-request latency.
- KV cache size growth past expected quantiles (per-model/per-pool).
- Increased retry rates and 5xx ratios from worker.
- Traces showing allocation peaks during specific kernels (attention, ff).

Mitigation ladder (ordered, earliest to last-resort):
1) Admission controls (pre-execution):
   - Reject or reject-with-suggestion requests exceeding per-model max_token_limits or sequence_length caps.
   - Per-customer soft quotas for long sequences; return 413-like structured error pointing to batchless suggestion.
2) Request-level preflight & circuit checks:
   - Preflight token estimate: multiply prompt-length + requested max_tokens by model factor; if estimate > threshold for pool, route to high-memory pool or return user-facing hint.
   - Consult per-pool circuit-breaker state (closed/half-open/open) before scheduling.
3) Dynamic kernel selection:
   - Prefer low-memory kernel variants if pool memory < threshold e.g., switch attention kernel to memory-efficient implementation.
   - Track kernel success rate and revert to fast kernels when healthy.
4) Batch / scheduling adjustments:
   - Reduce batch size for new requests entering stressed workers.
   - Temporarily disable opportunistic coalescing for long-sequence work.
5) KV cache eviction & trimming:
   - Evict least-recently-used prefixes below a freshness threshold.
   - Serve short-lived sessions with non-persistent cache (saves memory).
6) Model-variant fallback:
   - Canary fallback to quantized or smaller model variant (e.g., 8-bit or distillation) with a controlled percent of traffic.
   - Use quality guardrails: sample evals to monitor regression.
7) CPU fallback & streaming partial outputs:
   - If GPU allocation fails, attempt CPU worker fallback with early-token streaming; set pragmatic max_tokens to cap cost.
8) Soft circuit-open for model/pool:
   - Open circuit if OOM-rate exceeds configured threshold (e.g., 1% of requests in 5m) and sustained for a window.
   - On open: reject new long requests, route to fallback pools or model variants.
9) Emergency pool-level restart:
   - Controlled restart of worker process to clear fragmentation; schedule staggered restarts across nodes to preserve capacity.
10) Cluster-level emergency:
   - Spin up dedicated high-memory nodes or route to dedicated capacity (Reserved/Dedicated) as configured.

Circuit-breaker design (per-pool & per-model):
- States: CLOSED, HALF_OPEN, OPEN.
- Metrics: OOM_rate (OOMs / requests), 5xx_rate, avg_memory_headroom.
- Tripping rules (example):
  - If OOM_rate > 0.5% and OOM_count >= 10 in last 10 min AND avg_memory_headroom < 15% -> OPEN.
  - During OPEN: reject requests with helpful structured error code, route sample traffic to HALF_OPEN variants for probing.
  - HALF_OPEN probing: allow small percentage (1-5%) of requests, monitor fresh OOMs; on success -> CLOSE, on failures -> back to OPEN with exponential backoff.
- Scope: circuits exist at model-version-in-pool granularity and a pool-global fallback circuit.

Retry semantics and idempotency:
- Default: no automatic retry for non-idempotent generation calls at the routing layer.
- Safe retries allowed when: requests are marked idempotent OR when user asked for 'best-effort' with explicit retry policy.
- When retrying after OOM: use incremental mitigation (lowered max_tokens or different model-variant) and jittered backoff to avoid thundering herd.
- Retry budget: small fixed number (1 retry) with increasing fallback severity (e.g., reduce batch-size, switch kernel, switch model).

KV-cache specific tactics:
- Per-session budgets: limit per-session cached KV bytes; evict oldest sessions when over budget.
- Prefetch policy: avoid prefetching large KV slices for speculative completions.
- Sharded cache accounting: maintain approximate memory accounting per shard to allow localized eviction without global pauses.
- Cache compaction: coalesce small KV blocks to mitigate fragmentation periodically during low load windows.

Scheduling interactions & fairness:
- Classify requests by memory-intensity (short/prefix-only; long/decoder-heavy).
- Separate queues for low-memory requests vs high-memory requests to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Priority tiers (e.g., system-critical, enterprise-SLA, best-effort) with strict admission thresholds.
- Scheduler should be able to preempt queued best-effort requests when memory headroom dips below threshold.

Observability and telemetry (must have):
- Events: allocation_fail, kernel_abort, worker_restart, circuit_trip, kv_eviction, fallback_triggered.
- Traces: include allocation stack and kernel id in span tags; correlate with request_id and model_version.
- Dashboards: OOM-rate per pool, avg_memory_headroom, eviction_rate, fallback_rate, retry_count distribution.
- Alerts: page on sustained OOM_rate above SLO (configurable), or when circuit_open_count > 0 for critical models.

SRE runbook (incident steps):
1) Triage: identify scope (single worker, pool, cluster).
2) If single worker: check worker logs for kernel aborts; if crash loop -> cordon and restart worker, mark pool degradation.
3) If pool-level: increase fallback-routing to quantized variants (automated), reduce batch targets, enable low-memory kernels.
4) If cluster-level: communicate to growth/autoscaler to bring up high-memory nodes; temporarily open circuit to prevent downstream cascade.
5) Post-incident: collect memprof samples, annotate model profile, update model memory profile registry if we observed higher-than-expected working set.

Developer guidelines for model onboarding (to avoid future OOMs):
- Provide memory profile artifacts (psutil-style traces for synthetic sequences) as part of model bundle.
- Declare expected 95th percentile sequence lengths and preferred kernel dialects.
- Include a small quantized variant where possible and a test hook to exercise fallbacks.

Testing & chaos exercises:
- Unit tests: simulate kernel OOM error codes and assert circuit transitions and fallback behaviors.
- Load test: run synthetic long-seq workload to validate eviction and admission mechanisms.
- Chaos: inject artificial allocation failures on subset of nodes and ensure routing-level fallbacks keep 99th percentile of short requests within SLA.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Exact numeric thresholds for circuit tripping need calibration per-hardware class (A100-80GB vs 80GB V100).
- Backpressure propagation: how to signal upstream (API/SDK) to reduce client retry rates gracefully.
- Should we support automatic model slimming (on-the-fly token cap based on recent memory telemetry)?
- Define user-facing error codes for various mitigation states (e.g., MODEL_FALLBACK, RATE_LIMITED_FOR_MEMORY).

Appendix: quick examples
- Example: kernel OOM on attention for seq_len=4096 in pool-alpha
  Detection: CUDA OOM returned, OOM_rate spike, avg_memory_headroom 8%
  Automated actions (in order): switch to memory-efficient attention kernel -> reduce incoming batch size by 50% -> evict stale KV sessions -> open pool circuit -> route 10% traffic to quantized variant -> if still failing, mark pool degraded and spin up high-mem nodes.

- Example: KV cache growth steady over 30m exceeding budget
  Detection: eviction_rate high, per-session KV bytes > configured budget for many sessions
  Actions: mark long sessions as non-persistent, evict LRU sessions until back under budget, throttle new long-session admits, schedule cache compaction at off-peak window.

Notes for implementers: keep mitigation primitives small and composable (admission, kernel_tweak, eviction, model_fallback, cpu_fallback, circuit). Orchestration should allow composing these in different sequences per pool and enable rapid A/Bing of mitigations for tuning.

This is a living draft — please add examples from recent incidents (SERV-1172) and calibrate thresholds per instance type.
